planting.note: Divide clumps into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite bog mix, watering only with distilled or rain water in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium that must never receive fertilizer.

directions: DC-XL is an American-bred giant-trap Venus flytrap selection whose traps can approach two inches long, rising on tall, stout petioles that rival cultivars such as 'B52' and 'Ginormous' for sheer size. As with the wild-type species, each trap snaps shut in milliseconds when trigger hairs inside the lobes are touched twice in quick succession, sealing to digest captured insects over about a week. Grow it in a 1:1 peat and perlite or pure sphagnum mix watered only with rain or distilled water, since minerals in tap water and any fertilizer will quickly kill it. Give it full sun and a cool 3-to-4-month winter dormancy near 50°F to keep the clone vigorous and producing its outsized traps year after year.

planting.note: Divide slow-growing rosettes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite bog mix kept wet with rain or distilled water only; this nutrient-poor, unfertilized medium is essential.

directions: French-bred and named for the shapeshifting korrigan sprites of Breton folklore, this slow-growing, distinctly odd cultivar has trap lobes that merge into the leaf petiole instead of narrowing to a clear hinge, giving each leaf an almost fused, sculptural look even though the traps still snap and digest prey normally. Mature clumps stay compact, reaching only a few inches across, and produce small white spring flowers typical of the species. Grow it exactly as any Venus flytrap: pure sphagnum or a peat-perlite mix, rain or distilled water only, bright full sun, and a cool winter rest to keep the unusual form expressing strongly.
sources: European carnivorous plant nursery cultivar descriptions

planting.note: Divide clumps into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite bog mix watered only with rain or distilled water; the nutrient-poor, unfertilized medium mimics its native Carolina pine savanna.

directions: Selected from the coastal plain of the Carolinas, this cultivar is named for its marginal teeth, which fuse and cross over one another along each lobe rather than lining up in the usual comb-like row. Traps reach roughly four inches across, develop a deep reddish interior in strong light, and grow upright through summer before flattening into a low winter rosette during dormancy. Propagate only by division, since seed-grown offspring will not reliably show the crossed-tooth trait, and grow it under the same rules as any flytrap: sphagnum or peat-perlite medium, rain or distilled water, full sun, and a cool winter rest.
sources: European carnivorous plant nursery cultivar descriptions

planting.note: Root leaf pullings in a mineral mix of peat and perlite kept in low-mineral water; this hybrid still needs the acidic, nutrient-poor conditions of its Mexican Pinguicula parents even though it tolerates drier winters than bog-type carnivores.

directions: A popular hybrid between Pinguicula ehlersiae and Pinguicula moranensis, Sethos forms a flat rosette of broad, sticky-surfaced leaves that flush a vivid pink under strong light and trap small gnats and fungus flies on their glistening mucilage. It sends up wiry stalks of light purple flowers above the foliage during active growth. Like its Mexican highland parents, it wants very bright filtered light, a peat-and-perlite mix kept evenly moist with low-mineral rain or distilled water, and a 2-to-3-month winter rest with reduced watering as it drops its large summer leaves for a smaller, tighter rosette. Never fertilize the soil or water with hard tap water, since mineral buildup damages the roots.

planting.note: Root leaf pullings in a well-drained mineral mix of sand, perlite, and a little peat; keep the nutrient-poor soil evenly moist with rain or distilled water through the carnivorous growing season.

directions: Native to limestone outcrops in northeastern Mexico, this small butterwort is heterophyllous, switching between two very different leaf forms through the year. In the growing season it produces flat, round, sticky-glandular leaves that trap gnats and small insects, then contracts into a tight rosette of small, non-carnivorous succulent leaves to sit out the dry season. Single pink to lavender flowers appear on thin stalks above the summer rosette. Grow it in a mineral, well-drained mix watered with rain or distilled water, letting the medium dry slightly between waterings during its resting phase, and never add fertilizer.

common_name: Marston Dragon Sundew (Giant Forked-Leaf Sundew Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide root cuttings or crowns into a peat-perlite bog mix or pure sphagnum moss kept permanently wet with rain or distilled water; this nutrient-poor, unfertilized medium is essential for a carnivorous sundew.

directions: Bred by British carnivorous plant grower Adrian Slack from two forms of the Australian forked sundew, Marston Dragon produces dramatically branched, multiply-forking leaves that uncoil into a fountain-like rosette 12 inches or more across, each thin arm bristling with sticky red tentacles that curl around trapped gnats and small flies. It is one of the largest and showiest sundews grown outdoors, tolerating cooler conditions and a light winter dormancy better than most tropical Drosera. Grow it in a peat-perlite mix or pure sphagnum moss kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water, in full sun for the strongest tentacle color, and propagate true-to-type divisions by root cuttings since it is a sterile or unreliable-from-seed clonal hybrid.

planting.note: Root leaf cuttings or set divisions into a 1:1 peat-sand mix kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; this nutrient-poor, acidic soil should never be fertilized.

directions: Described in 1987 from the southwestern Cape of South Africa, this compact rosette sundew holds a single tight cluster of rounded, wedge-shaped leaves whose outer tentacles bend inward within minutes of snaring a gnat or other tiny insect. Small five-petaled, light-violet flowers with bright yellow anthers open for just one morning at a time on short stalks above the foliage. Unlike temperate sundews, it grows year-round without a winter dormancy, so keep it evenly warm, in a deep pot of peat and sand kept wet with rain or distilled water, and in bright light for the deepest red tentacle color.

planting.note: Press divisions or existing sod onto the surface of a wet peat-sand mix or pure milled sphagnum kept constantly saturated with rain or distilled water; never use fertilizer or tap water on this nutrient-poor substrate.

directions: Native to wet savanna sands of Brazil, Guyana, Venezuela, and Suriname, this terrestrial bladderwort produces teardrop-shaped leaves streaked with purple veins and captures microscopic soil organisms with tiny underground bladder traps rather than visible leaf structures. It blooms nearly year-round without a dormancy requirement, sending up thin, wiry stalks topped with rosy-purple flowers marked with yellow. Keep it in shallow trays of wet, nutrient-poor peat-sand mix or milled sphagnum under bright indirect light or humid greenhouse conditions, watering only with rain or distilled water, and it will spread steadily by fine rhizomes to fill a pot.
